text:
A two-time Kentucky Derby winner was refused the front door of a Louisville hotel in 1961 at a banquet being held in his honor. Jimmy Winkfield stood on the sidewalk at Fourth and Broadway in a pin-striped suit with his daughter beside him while men upstairs waited to applaud him.

He had ridden for the Tsar of Russia and walked two hundred and sixty racehorses eleven hundred miles across a war to save them.

Louisville gave him a doorway he was not allowed to use.

The old man came up Fourth Street in a pin-striped suit and a fedora, with his daughter on his arm, and stopped at the front door of the Brown Hotel.

It was May of 1961. Inside, on an upper floor, a banquet room was filling with the best turf writers in America, and the dinner was being given in his honor.

Sports Illustrated had paid to fly him in from France. It had been fifty-eight years since he had last seen Louisville.

He was told he could not come in that way.

The man who told him, by one account, was the hotel's own doorman. A Black man in a uniform, doing the job the hotel paid him to do, standing in the one spot where the rule had to be said out loud.

So the two of them waited on the sidewalk at Fourth and Broadway. A man near eighty years old and his grown daughter, who had been raised in France and had never been refused a door in her life.

Somebody eventually went and found the magazine's people, and there were arguments. The organizers came down, the hotel relented, and the guest of honor was allowed to walk into the building where a room full of men were waiting to applaud him.

When he came in, most of the room found something else to look at.

One man crossed the floor to him. Roscoe Goose was white, and he had won the 1913 Kentucky Derby on a horse called Donerail at ninety-one to one, which is still the longest price ever to win that race.

The rest let him stand there.

His name was Jimmy Winkfield.

He had won the Kentucky Derby in 1901. He won it again in 1902, and no Black rider has won it since.

He was born in Chilesburg, outside Lexington, the youngest of seventeen children on a sharecropper's place. Sources put the year at 1880 or 1882, and nobody has ever settled it.

His first professional ride was a catastrophe. On a horse named Jockey Joe at Hawthorne in Chicago in 1898, he broke fourth from the rail and cut hard across three horses on the inside, and all four went down.

The stewards suspended him for a year.

He was sixteen.

He came back in September of 1899 at the Harlem track outside Chicago and won. Then he won thirty-eight more times that season, and the May brothers signed him to a three-year contract.

Col. Phil Chinn, a fixture of the Bluegrass horse establishment, watched him come up and said Bub May never had to teach that boy anything. The kid had no particular style, Chinn said, he just sat up there like a piece of gold.

In 1900 he rode a colt called Thrive in his first Kentucky Derby and finished third. It was the first of four Derby rides, and no jockey since has bettered what he did across those four.

That same year he went to New York looking for mounts. White riders there had organized what they were calling an anti-colored union, and the Black jockeys he had grown up admiring were standing around the backstretch unable to get work.

He went back to Chicago, and at the Harlem track a white jockey ran him into the rail.

He got up with a badly bruised leg. The horse had cracked ribs.

That was the method, and there was nothing unusual about it. Charles Parmer set the whole thing down in his 1939 history of American racing.

A Black rider would get pocketed and shoved back through the field. Or bumped off his line, or run wide, or a man would come alongside, hook a boot under his stirrup and lift him out of the saddle at speed.

Or the man beside you swung his whip wide while appearing to urge his own horse, and opened your face.

From the grandstand it read as a rough trip, and a steward saw nothing but racing. An owner saw an expensive animal come back sore and quietly hired somebody else the following week.

The New York Times put it plainly on 29 July 1900. The public believed the old Black riders had lost their touch, the paper reported, and racing men knew better, because a quietly formed combination had shut them out.

Winkfield was twenty years old, riding into that, and he had two Kentucky Derbies in front of him.

He took the first one in 1901 on His Eminence and led the whole way. He won a hundred and sixty-one races that year.

The second one is the ride they should still be teaching.

On 3 May 1902 he went to the front on a chestnut colt named Alan-a-Dale, owned, bred and trained by Thomas Clay McDowell, a great-grandson of Henry Clay. The colt was unsound and everyone in the barn knew it.

Winkfield opened up six lengths. Then, in the stretch, the horse went lame underneath him.

A rider gets a few seconds to decide a thing like that. Pull him up and save the animal, or hold him together and try to steal the biggest race in America on a leg that is coming apart.

He held him together.

He drifted the closers out toward the deep, slow going in the middle of the track. He kept the colt balanced and moving, and Alan-a-Dale went under the wire by a nose.

The horse did not race again that year.

Winkfield was twenty or twenty-two, depending on which birth year you believe. He had won the Kentucky Derby twice running, something only Isaac Murphy had ever done, and nobody would match it again until Ron Turcotte on Riva Ridge and Secretariat seventy years later.

He was making a thousand dollars a race. He had started at eight dollars a month.

Then it ended, and it ended over a horse race that was not the Derby.

Winkfield had given his word to John E. Madden, one of the most powerful owners in American racing, that he would ride Madden's horse in the Futurity. He took another man's mount instead.

Breaking a verbal commitment was a real offence and white jockeys did it too. What happened next was not what happened to them.

Madden went to every prominent owner he could reach and told them not to put Winkfield up. The number is in the record: three hundred and ninety-one mounts in 1902, two hundred and twenty-three in 1903.

He rode the odds-on favorite Early in the 1903 Kentucky Derby, took a lead of a length and a half, and got caught in the stretch and beaten by three-quarters of a length. He called it the worst loss of his life.

There was also the Klan, which had started sending him threats.

At the end of 1903 he bought a steamer ticket. He was twenty-one years old, he had a Russian-Polish-English dictionary, and he did not speak a word of any of it.

Russia decided he was magnificent.

He won the Emperor's Purse and the Russian Oaks five times and the Warsaw Derby, and by the middle of it he was earning something like a hundred thousand dollars a year in rubles. He kept a suite in the best hotel in Moscow and he employed a white valet.

He came back across the Atlantic to visit in December of 1909, and the New York Sun noticed how he had travelled. The headline read that a gentleman from Kentucky had come second class so as not to vex the intolerant.

A man who kept a suite in Moscow and dined with counts had booked himself onto the cheap deck for the crossing home. He had worked out exactly what an American ship would tolerate from him and he had priced it in advance.

In Russia he rode for Armenian oil money and sat for photographs in the newspapers. In America he was a Black man who knew which deck to buy.

Then, in 1917, the aristocracy stopped existing.

Racing died with it. Winkfield followed the Moscow racing crowd nine hundred miles south to Odessa, on the Black Sea, where a Polish horseman named Frederick Jurjevich had built a refuge from the war.

It lasted two more years.

On the morning of 4 April 1919, Winkfield woke to the sound of artillery on the edge of the city.

He was thirty-seven, or thirty-nine. Years later he said what he had thought lying there listening to it, which was that this was no longer a fit place for a small colored man from Chilesburg, Kentucky, to be.

Jurjevich had a plan and the plan was insane. Get the whole racing colony out overland, west and north to Warsaw, roughly eleven hundred miles across a continent that had just finished tearing itself apart.

Men, women and children. And two hundred and sixty racehorses.

Winkfield was made his second in command. He said he was damned if he was going to leave the horses behind to be eaten.

They walked.

Out of Ukraine, over the Transylvanian Alps, through what is now Romania and Hungary. A column carrying the most valuable bloodstock left in Russia and the people who had bred it, moving at the pace of a horse that cannot be hurried.

There was no food to buy. Villagers along the route robbed them, and in some places they staged races in the road to raise money to keep going.

It took three months.

Winkfield brought that column into Warsaw having lost eight or ten horses out of two hundred and sixty.

He was a jockey. He had been handed the most valuable horses left in Europe, a column of families, and a war to walk them across.

He rebuilt in France. There was a wife, a chateau with private stables in Maisons-Laffitte outside Paris, a training operation, and by the time he stopped riding in 1930 he had somewhere over two thousand six hundred wins to his name.

In 1940 the Germans came.

They took the property. One account has him facing them down in his own stable yard holding a pitchfork.

He got out with his family and reached New York in 1941, close to sixty years old. What America had for him was a jackhammer on a Works Progress Administration crew, and after that a job with the Bostwick stable at Aiken, South Carolina, working horses for wages.

The man who had ridden for the Tsar spent the war years mucking out in South Carolina.

He went back to France in 1953, reopened his stables, and started a school to teach young riders. Then in 1961 a magazine offered to bring him home for the Derby, and he took it, and he brought Liliane.

Which is how a two-time Kentucky Derby winner came to be standing on the pavement at Fourth and Broadway in the state where he was born, in a good suit, being told which entrance was his.

Three days later he sat in a box at Churchill Downs and watched the race as a spectator.

He went back to Maisons-Laffitte. He told people he had thought about selling up and moving home to America for good.

He never came back.

He died in France in March of 1974, ninety-one or ninety-three years old. American racing took another thirty years to say his name properly.

On 9 August 2004 the National Museum of Racing put him in the Hall of Fame at Saratoga Springs. Someone had to walk up and accept the plaque for him, and the person who did it was Liliane Winkfield Casey.

The same daughter. The one who had stood beside him on the sidewalk in Louisville forty-three years earlier while men decided whether her father could use a door.

Behind him the gate emptied out fast. Jess Conley brought a horse home third in 1911, the last Black rider ever to finish in the money.

Henry King finished tenth in 1921. Nobody in the stands understood they had just watched the last one for a lifetime.

The next Black man to get a Derby mount was Marlon St. Julien, of Lafayette, Louisiana, who rode a colt called Curule to seventh place in the year 2000. Seventy-nine years had passed.

Four Black riders have made it into that gate since 1921.

Since Alan-a-Dale came home lame and first in 1902, none of them has won.

There is a race for him now. Every January at Aqueduct in Queens, on the Monday they set aside for Martin Luther King, they run six furlongs and call it the Jimmy Winkfield Stakes.

Six furlongs on a cold morning in New York, for a man who won nearly every race worth winning in Europe and could not get through the front door of a hotel in the state where he was born.

text:
Minneapolis restaurant that offered free meals to protest ICE raids announces closure
Owner Dylan Alverson says he 'exhausted every option' after trying to keep Minnesota establishment operational 

Modern Times Café, a Minneapolis restaurant that attempted to eliminate prices, has announced it will be closing for good by the end of the year.

"For the last six years, I’ve been trying to prove that Modern Times can continue to exist," owner Dylan Alverson wrote on social media Saturday. "I’ve exhausted every option without compromising the core fundamentals that make Modern Times what it is."

He added that he plans to spend the next two months celebrating the 16-year-old business and discussing ways for a business like his to continue.

"The only way for places like Modern Times to exist in the future is to actively challenge the reasons why it can no longer exist," Alverson wrote.

Alverson announced on Instagram in January that his business, which rebranded as Post Modern Times, would operate as a "free and donation-based restaurant" where everyone would be welcome "except ICE" in protest of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations happening in his state, partly in response to the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

text:
31 items in my cart at self-checkout in Moore, Oklahoma.

One $12 pack of batteries did not scan.
Loss prevention stopped me and walked me to a back office.

Him: "Sign this admission and we do not call the police."
Me: "What does the form say?"
Him: "It says you intended to steal the twelve-dollar batteries."
Me: "I missed one scan out of thirty-one items. I can pay for them right now."
Him: "Just sign the form."

Me: "I am happy to pay for the batteries, but I am not signing that."

Under 22 O.S. 1343, an Oklahoma merchant may detain a person in a reasonable manner for a reasonable length of time to investigate suspected shoplifting.
Signing a store confession or admission form is completely optional.
Under 21 O.S. 1701, Oklahoma defines larceny as taking personal property accomplished by fraud or stealth, "with intent to deprive another thereof."

Criminal intent is a required element of the crime.
Under 21 O.S. 1731, larceny of merchandise valued under $1,000 carries up to 30 days in county jail on a first conviction.
A missed barcode scan does not prove criminal intent.
A signed confession hands over the one element the missed scan alone never proved.
You can stay calm, offer to pay for the item and decline to sign.
P.S. Look up 21 O.S. 1701 and read the last six words.

If you or someone in your family is facing a charge like this in Oklahoma, start here. We'll help, or help you find someone who can: https://t.co/WgXb7b6bMg
